steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on multi-objective optimization for training sparse deep multi-task networks. Motivate optimizing several objectives (like accuracy and model size) at once, explain the limits of existing multi-objective methods for deep learning, introduce our approach, and give the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Single-loss DNN training vs. multi-objective optimization; conflicting objectives and the Pareto set
- Limits of weighted sums and of existing MOO methods for deep learning
- Our approach: Weighted Chebyshev + Augmented Lagrangian; sparsity for multi-task models
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - Deep Learning: remarkable success across many applications
  - standard DNN training minimizes a single loss (empirical loss)
  - ignores benefits of optimizing several objectives at once: model size, computational complexity, accuracy across tasks
  - MOO in training: balance conflicting objectives, broader exploration of DNN parameterizations; optimal trade-offs
  - examples: smaller model -> lower accuracy; better performance -> more complexity
  - ignoring trade-offs limits versatile, efficient models across tasks
  - MOO finds optimal compromises = Pareto set, each parameterization a unique trade-off
  - exploring it: insight into how objectives relate, informed design and parameter choices
- Existing methods
  - weighted sum: convex combination; assumes convexity, misses non-convex parts of Pareto front
  - weights for more than two objectives hard and subjective
  - non-convex: advanced scalarization, gradient-based, evolutionary, set-oriented
  - evolutionary and set-oriented too expensive in DL (many function evaluations)
  - gradient-based popular, cost like single-objective, but give a single Pareto solution -> not for decision-makers wanting several trade-offs
- Our approach
  - Weighted Chebyshev (WC) scalarization + Augmented Lagrangian (AL) for the sequence of scalar problems
  - efficient computation of entire Pareto set; trade-off environment = optimal parameterizations of a DNN
  - model complexity reduction as extra objective -> sustainability of DNNs, focus on Deep Multi-Task models
  - adaptively sparsify during training, efficiency without much loss in performance
  - experiments on two datasets
- Organization
  - Section 2 related work on MOO for DNN training
  - Section 3 methodology: modified WC scalarization, AL, Group Ordered Weighted l_{1} (GrOWL) for smaller models
  - Section 4 results on two datasets
  - Section 5 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep Learning has changed many fields and has had remarkable success in a wide range of applications. The standard way of training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is to minimize one loss function, usually the empirical loss, to improve the performance of the model. This works, but it ignores the possible benefits of optimizing several objectives at the same time, for example making the model smaller and less computationally complex while keeping a good level of accuracy across different tasks. To deal with this limitation, a Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) framework can be used in the training of DNNs, so that we find a balance between conflicting objectives and explore DNN parameterizations more completely. In this way several criteria are optimized at the same time and we can train DNNs that have optimal trade-offs among these objectives.

In Deep Learning there are several situations where we have to consider trade-offs between objectives that conflict with each other. For example, making the model smaller can cost some accuracy, and improving the model performance can make the model more complex. If these trade-offs are neglected, it is harder to develop DNN models that are versatile and efficient and that do well across various tasks. Instead, Multi-Objective Optimization tries to find optimal compromises, called the Pareto set, which is a collection of parameterizations of a DNN where each one gives a different trade-off between the objectives. When we explore the Pareto set, we get useful insights into how the different objectives relate to each other, and we can make informed decisions about model design and parameter selection.

- Existing methods
  - weighted sum: convex combination; assumes convexity, misses non-convex parts of Pareto front; weights for more than two objectives hard and subjective
  - non-convex: advanced scalarization, gradient-based, evolutionary, set-oriented
  - evolutionary and set-oriented too expensive in DL; gradient-based cheap but give a single Pareto solution
- Our approach
  - Weighted Chebyshev (WC) scalarization + Augmented Lagrangian (AL); entire Pareto set efficiently
  - model complexity as extra objective -> sustainability, Deep Multi-Task models; adaptive sparsification during training
  - experiments on two datasets
- Organization
  - Section 2 related work; Section 3 modified WC, AL, Group Ordered Weighted l_{1} (GrOWL); Section 4 results on two datasets; Section 5 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep Learning has changed many fields and has had remarkable success in a wide range of applications. The standard way of training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is to minimize one loss function, usually the empirical loss, to improve the performance of the model. This works, but it ignores the possible benefits of optimizing several objectives at the same time, for example making the model smaller and less computationally complex while keeping a good level of accuracy across different tasks. To deal with this limitation, a Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) framework can be used in the training of DNNs, so that we find a balance between conflicting objectives and explore DNN parameterizations more completely. In this way several criteria are optimized at the same time and we can train DNNs that have optimal trade-offs among these objectives.

In Deep Learning there are several situations where we have to consider trade-offs between objectives that conflict with each other. For example, making the model smaller can cost some accuracy, and improving the model performance can make the model more complex. If these trade-offs are neglected, it is harder to develop DNN models that are versatile and efficient and that do well across various tasks. Instead, Multi-Objective Optimization tries to find optimal compromises, called the Pareto set, which is a collection of parameterizations of a DNN where each one gives a different trade-off between the objectives. When we explore the Pareto set, we get useful insights into how the different objectives relate to each other, and we can make informed decisions about model design and parameter selection.

The traditional methods for multiple criteria in optimization often use weighted sum approaches, where the objectives are combined into a convex combination. But this assumes convexity and cannot capture non-convex parts of the Pareto front, so it is limited in complex optimization problems. Also, choosing good weights for more than two objectives gets more and more difficult and subjective. So for non-convex problems we need more advanced techniques, such as sophisticated scalarization techniques, gradient-based approaches, evolutionary algorithms, or set-oriented techniques. In Deep Learning, evolutionary algorithms and set-oriented methods are both too expensive, because they need a very large number of function evaluations. Gradient-based methods have become popular since their computational cost is comparable to single-objective problems. But these methods usually give only one solution on the Pareto set, so they are not suitable when a decision-maker wants to see several possible trade-offs.

To handle the challenges of non-convex problems and conflicting objectives, we propose to use a more advanced scalarization approach, the Weighted Chebyshev (WC) scalarization, together with the Augmented Lagrangian (AL) method to solve the sequence of scalar optimization problems that results from it. With our method the entire Pareto set can be computed efficiently, which lets us explore the trade-off environment (i.e. the optimal parameterizations of a DNN model) comprehensively. We also treat reducing model complexity as an additional objective function, so this study also tries to address the sustainability issue of DNN models, especially Deep Multi-Task models. In particular, we look at whether it is feasible to sparsify the model adaptively during training to reduce its complexity and make it more computationally efficient, without hurting the performance of the model too much. We run experiments on two datasets to evaluate how effective this method is.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. In Section 2 we review related works on Multi-Objective Optimization for Deep Neural Network Training. Section 3 presents the methodology, with a detailed description of a modified WC scalarization method, the AL approach, and the Group Ordered Weighted l_{1} (GrOWL) function, which helps to reduce the model size. Section 4 gives the results we obtained on two different datasets. Section 5 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep Learning has revolutionized various fields, achieving remarkable success across a wide range of applications. The standard approach to training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is to minimize a single loss function, typically the empirical loss, to improve model performance. While effective, this approach disregards the potential benefits of simultaneously optimizing multiple objectives, such as reducing model size and computational complexity while maintaining a desirable level of accuracy across different tasks. To address this limitation, a Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) framework can be incorporated into the training process of DNNs, aiming to balance conflicting objectives and enable a more comprehensive exploration of DNN parameterizations. This allows multiple criteria to be optimized simultaneously and facilitates training DNNs with optimal trade-offs among these objectives. In Deep Learning, several scenarios require trade-offs between inherently conflicting objectives. For instance, reducing model size may come at the cost of decreased accuracy, while improving model performance may increase model complexity. Neglecting these trade-offs limits the ability to develop versatile and efficient DNN models that excel across various tasks. Instead, Multi-Objective Optimization aims to identify optimal compromises, denoted as the Pareto set: a collection of DNN parameterizations, each offering a unique trade-off between objectives. Exploring the Pareto set gives valuable insights into the interrelationship of the objectives and supports informed decisions about model design and parameter selection.

Traditional methods for handling multiple criteria often rely on weighted sum approaches, in which objectives are combined into a convex combination. However, this approach assumes convexity and fails to capture non-convex sections of the Pareto front, which limits its effectiveness in complex optimization scenarios [1,2]. Moreover, choosing appropriate weights for more than two objectives becomes increasingly difficult and subjective. For non-convex problems, we thus need more advanced techniques such as sophisticated scalarization techniques [2], gradient-based approaches [3], evolutionary algorithms [4], or set-oriented techniques [5,6]. In Deep Learning, both evolutionary algorithms and set-oriented methods are too expensive, since they require a very large number of function evaluations. Gradient-based methods have gained popularity because their computational efficiency is comparable to single-objective problems. However, they typically yield a single solution on the Pareto set, which makes them unsuitable when a decision-maker is interested in multiple possible trade-offs. To tackle the challenges of non-convex problems and conflicting objectives, we propose a more advanced scalarization approach, the Weighted Chebyshev (WC) scalarization, combined with the Augmented Lagrangian (AL) method to solve the resulting sequence of scalar optimization problems. Our methodology enables efficient computation of the entire Pareto set, allowing a comprehensive exploration of the trade-off environment (i.e. the optimal parameterizations of a DNN model). By treating the reduction of model complexity as an additional objective function, this study also addresses the sustainability issue of DNN models, with a particular focus on Deep Multi-Task models. Specifically, we investigate whether the model can be adaptively sparsified during training to reduce complexity and gain computational efficiency without significantly compromising performance. We evaluate the effectiveness of this method in experiments on two datasets.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related works in Multi-Objective Optimization for Deep Neural Network Training. Section 3 presents the methodology, with a detailed description of a modified WC scalarization method, the AL approach, and the Group Ordered Weighted l_{1} (GrOWL) function, which facilitates the reduction of model size. Section 4 presents the results obtained on two distinct datasets. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper.

References:
[1] K. Bieker, B. Gebken, and S. Peitz, “On the treatment of optimization problems with l1 penalty terms via multiobjective continuation,” IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence , vol. 44, no. 11, pp. 7797–7808, 2021.
[2] K. Miettinen, Nonlinear multiobjective optimization . Springer Science & Business Media, 1999, vol. 12.
[3] J. Fliege and B. F. Svaiter, “Steepest descent methods for multicriteria optimization,” Mathematical methods of operations research , vol. 51, pp. 479–494, 2000.
[4] C. A. C. Coello, A. H. Aguirre, and E. Zitzler, Evolutionary multi-criterion optimization . Springer, 2005.
[5] S. Peitz and M. Dellnitz, “Gradient-based multiobjective optimization with uncertainties,” in NEO 2016: Results of the Numerical and Evolutionary Optimization Workshop NEO 2016 and the NEO Cities 2016 Workshop held on September 20-24, 2016 in Tlalnepantla, Mexico . Springer, 2018, pp. 159–182.
[6] M. Dellnitz, O. Schütze, and T. Hestermeyer, “Covering pareto sets by multilevel subdivision techniques,” Journal of optimization theory and applications , vol. 124, pp. 113–136, 2005.
